questions.stem: How are electromagnetic waves produced?
options: By a steady magnetic field acting on a charge that is held at rest
By sound waves making the electrons in the air vibrate back and forth
By accelerating charges, which make changing electric and magnetic fields
By charges moving at a constant velocity along a straight conductor
questions.explanation: An accelerating charge produces a changing electric field, which produces a changing magnetic field, and so on: the two fields sustain each other and travel as an electromagnetic wave. A charge moving at constant velocity, or a static field, does not radiate.

questions.stem: In an electromagnetic wave travelling through a vacuum, how do the electric and magnetic fields oscillate?
options: Parallel to each other and to the direction of travel
Parallel to the direction of travel, as in a sound wave
At right angles to each other, with E along the direction of travel
At right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
questions.explanation: Light is a transverse wave: both fields oscillate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, and perpendicular to each other. Oscillation along the direction of travel would make it a longitudinal wave, like sound.

questions.stem: Which property is the same for every type of electromagnetic wave travelling through a vacuum?
options: Photon energy
Speed
Frequency
Wavelength
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum at c, 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Frequency, wavelength and photon energy all differ across the spectrum; a higher frequency comes with a shorter wavelength so that their product is always c.

questions.stem: A mobile phone network transmits at 900 MHz. What is the wavelength of its signal? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 9.0 × 10⁸ ≈ 0.33 m. Dividing the frequency by the speed gives 3.0, and multiplying them gives 2.7 × 10¹⁷, neither of which is a wavelength.

questions.stem: How does a standing wave form on a guitar string?
options: The string vibrates faster than the wave can travel along the string
A travelling wave superposes with its reflection from the fixed ends
Two waves of different frequencies travel along it in one direction
A single wave travels along the string without ever being reflected
questions.explanation: A wave reflected from a fixed end travels back and superposes with the incoming wave. At certain frequencies this produces fixed nodes and antinodes, a standing wave. Without reflection there is only a travelling wave.

questions.stem: In a standing wave, what is the distance between two adjacent nodes?
options: A quarter of a wavelength
Two wavelengths
Half a wavelength
One wavelength
questions.explanation: Nodes are spaced half a wavelength apart, with an antinode midway between each pair. The distance from a node to the next antinode is a quarter of a wavelength.

questions.stem: A string 0.60 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in a standing wave with three antinodes. What is the wavelength?
questions.explanation: Three antinodes means three half-wavelength loops fit along the string: 3 × λ/2 = 0.60 m, so λ = 0.40 m. Using a whole wavelength per loop gives 0.20 m, and 1.2 m is the wavelength of the fundamental, with one loop.

questions.stem: Waves travel at 240 m s⁻¹ on a string 0.80 m long that is fixed at both ends. What is the frequency of its second harmonic?
options: 150 Hz
600 Hz
75 Hz
300 Hz
questions.explanation: With nodes at both ends, the harmonics have f = nv/(2L). The fundamental is 240/(2 × 0.80) = 150 Hz, so the second harmonic is 300 Hz, with a wavelength equal to the string’s length. 150 Hz is the fundamental.

questions.stem: Diffraction of a wave through a gap is most noticeable when:
options: the frequency of the wave is made very much higher
the amplitude of the wave is much larger than the gap
the wavelength is similar to or larger than the gap width
the gap is very much wider than the wavelength of the wave
questions.explanation: The amount of diffraction depends on the ratio λ/w. When the wavelength is comparable to the gap width or larger, the wave spreads widely. A much higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, which reduces diffraction through the same gap.

questions.stem: Light of a single wavelength passes through a narrow slit, making a diffraction pattern on a screen. The slit is made narrower. What happens to the central bright band?
options: It becomes narrower, as less light gets through
It keeps its width, but becomes much dimmer
It becomes wider, because λ/w increases
It becomes narrower, because λ/w decreases
questions.explanation: A narrower slit increases the ratio λ/w, so the light spreads more and the central band widens. Less light does pass through, so the pattern dims, but the band does not narrow.

questions.stem: Why can visible light, of wavelength about 500 nm, not produce a sharp image of a virus 50 nm across?
options: Visible light travels too slowly to reflect from an object that small
With λ/w about 10, diffraction spreads the light too much to resolve the virus
With λ/w about 0.1, the light passes the virus without being affected at all
Visible light photons have too much energy, so they destroy the virus
questions.explanation: When the wavelength is much larger than the object, λ/w is large and the light diffracts strongly around it, so no sharp detail can form. Imaging small objects needs a wavelength comparable to or smaller than their size. Visible light photons carry only a few electron-volts.

questions.stem: Young’s double slit experiment provides evidence that light:
options: behaves as a wave, because it produces an interference pattern
is made of particles, because separate bright bands appear
travels at the same speed for all observers in all frames
is emitted in discrete packets of energy called photons
questions.explanation: Bright and dark bands form where waves from the two slits interfere constructively and destructively. Interference is a wave property, which is why Young’s result supported the wave model of light. The photon model came later, from the photoelectric effect.

questions.stem: In a double slit pattern, consider the third bright band to one side of the central bright band, not counting the central band. What is the path difference to it from the two slits?
options: 2λ
3λ
questions.explanation: Bright bands occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, nλ, with n = 0 at the central band. The third bright band beyond the centre has n = 3, so the path difference is 3λ. Half-integer values such as 2.5λ give dark bands.

questions.stem: In a double slit pattern, what is the path difference from the two slits to the second dark band on one side of the central bright band?
options: 2λ
questions.explanation: Dark bands occur where the path difference is (n − ½)λ, so the waves arrive half a cycle out of step. The first dark band is at 0.5λ and the second at 1.5λ. Whole-number values such as 2λ give bright bands.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.40 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. What is the spacing between adjacent bright bands?
options: 3.0 mm
30 mm
1.5 mm
questions.explanation: Δx = λL/d = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0)/(0.40 × 10⁻³) = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m = 3.0 mm. The other values come from slips in converting nanometres and millimetres, or from halving the spacing.

questions.stem: Which single change would double the spacing between bright bands in a double slit experiment?
options: Halving the separation of the slits
Halving the slit-to-screen distance
Halving the wavelength of the light
Doubling the separation of the slits
questions.explanation: Since Δx = λL/d, the spacing is inversely proportional to the slit separation, so halving d doubles Δx. Halving either L or λ would halve the spacing, and doubling d would also halve it.

questions.stem: In a double slit experiment, the bright bands are 2.4 mm apart on a screen 1.5 m from slits 0.25 mm apart. What is the wavelength of the light?
options: 400 nm
900 nm
200 nm
800 nm
questions.explanation: Rearranging Δx = λL/d gives λ = Δx d/L = (2.4 × 10⁻³ × 0.25 × 10⁻³)/1.5 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 400 nm. Multiplying all three quantities together gives 900 nm.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.0 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by f gives 1.3 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J, and 2.0 × 10⁻²⁵ is hc, which still needs dividing by a wavelength.

questions.stem: What is the energy, in electron-volts, of a photon of wavelength 620 nm? Use h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 2.0 eV
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ = (4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(620 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 2.0 eV. The value 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the same energy in joules, so attaching eV to it confuses the units.

questions.stem: Which observation of the photoelectric effect supports a particle model of light?
options: At low intensity, electrons are emitted only after a noticeable delay
The kinetic energy of the emitted electrons rises with the light’s intensity
Below a threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however bright the light
Light of any frequency releases electrons once it is made bright enough
questions.explanation: Each electron absorbs one photon, of energy hf. If hf is less than the work function, no single photon can free an electron, so more photons, meaning brighter light, makes no difference. The other statements are what the wave model predicted, and none was observed.

questions.stem: Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on a metal with a work function of 2.3 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons? Use h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s.
options: 2.3 eV
3.9 eV
8.5 eV
6.2 eV
questions.explanation: The photon energy is hf = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 6.2 eV, and Ek(max) = hf − φ = 6.2 − 2.3 = 3.9 eV. 6.2 eV forgets that the work function must be supplied first, and 8.5 eV adds it instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: The most energetic photoelectrons from a metal have 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J of kinetic energy. What stopping voltage brings the photocurrent to zero? Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: The stopping voltage removes all the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons: eV = Ek(max), so V = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5 V. Dividing the other way round gives 0.67 V.

questions.stem: On a graph of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against the frequency of the incident light, what do the gradient and the horizontal intercept represent?
options: The work function and the threshold frequency
Planck’s constant and the work function
The threshold frequency and Planck’s constant
Planck’s constant and the threshold frequency
questions.explanation: From Ek(max) = hf − φ, the graph is a straight line of gradient h. It crosses the frequency axis where Ek is zero, at the threshold frequency. The work function appears as the magnitude of the intercept on the vertical axis, not the horizontal one.

questions.stem: A graph of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency for sodium crosses the frequency axis at 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the work function of sodium? Use h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s.
options: 4.6 eV
2.3 eV
5.5 eV
questions.explanation: At the threshold frequency the photon energy just equals the work function: φ = hf₀ = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 5.5 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 2.3 eV. The value 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the same energy in joules, so labelling it in eV mixes up the units.

questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, the intensity of the light is doubled and its frequency kept the same. How does the graph of photocurrent against electrode potential change?
options: Its saturation current stays the same and its stopping voltage falls
Its saturation current doubles and its stopping voltage stays the same
Its saturation current stays the same and its stopping voltage doubles
Its saturation current doubles and its stopping voltage becomes larger
questions.explanation: Twice the intensity at the same frequency means twice as many photons, each of the same energy. So twice as many electrons are emitted, doubling the saturation current, but their maximum kinetic energy, and so the stopping voltage, is unchanged.

questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, the frequency of the light is increased while the number of photons arriving each second stays the same. How does the graph of photocurrent against electrode potential change?
options: A larger stopping voltage and a larger saturation current
A larger stopping voltage and the same saturation current
The same stopping voltage and a larger saturation current
A smaller stopping voltage and the same saturation current
questions.explanation: Higher-frequency photons carry more energy, so the photoelectrons have more kinetic energy and a larger stopping voltage is needed. With the same number of photons each second, the number of electrons emitted, and so the saturation current, does not change.

questions.stem: What did the wave model of light predict for the photoelectric effect that experiments did not show?
options: Emission would begin at once, even with very dim light
Light of any frequency would eject electrons if bright enough
No electrons would be ejected below a threshold frequency
Electron energy would depend only on the light’s frequency
questions.explanation: In the wave model, energy arrives continuously, so bright enough light of any frequency should eventually free electrons. Experiments showed a threshold frequency, energy depending only on frequency, and instant emission, which the photon model explains and the wave model cannot.

questions.stem: Light above the threshold frequency falls on a metal. Increasing the light’s intensity increases:
options: the number of photoelectrons emitted each second
the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
the work function of the metal’s surface
the threshold frequency of the metal
questions.explanation: Greater intensity at the same frequency means more photons per second, so more electrons are freed each second. Each photon still has energy hf, so the maximum kinetic energy does not change. The work function and threshold frequency are properties of the metal.

questions.stem: A beam of electrons passing through a thin metal foil produces a pattern of bright and dark rings. This is evidence that:
options: electrons have wave-like properties
electrons have particle-like properties
the foil emits photons when it is struck
electrons travel faster than light in metal
questions.explanation: Rings of constructive and destructive interference are a diffraction pattern, which only waves produce. That electrons diffract like X-rays confirmed de Broglie’s idea that matter has a wavelength.

questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and electron mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.0 × 10⁶) ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Using the proton’s mass gives 2.0 × 10⁻¹³ m, and 7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m comes from using ½mv as the momentum.

questions.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through 150 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and electron mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: Ek = qV = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, so p = √(2mEk) = √(2 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁷) ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹ and λ = h/p ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Leaving out the 2 gives 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and 8.3 × 10⁻⁹ m is the wavelength of a 150 eV photon, not an electron.

questions.stem: An X-ray beam and an electron beam produce identical diffraction patterns when passed through the same metal foil. Which statement is correct?
options: They have the same wavelength, but each X-ray photon has far more energy than each electron
They have the same energy per particle, so they must also have the same wavelength
They have the same wavelength, and each electron has far more energy than each photon
They have the same wavelength, but each electron has more momentum than each photon
questions.explanation: Identical patterns mean identical wavelengths, and since p = h/λ for both, identical momenta. A photon’s energy is pc, while a slow electron’s is p²/(2m), which is far smaller for the same momentum. So patterns can match even though the energies are very different.

questions.stem: Why can an electron microscope resolve much finer detail than a light microscope?
options: Its electrons have much shorter wavelengths, so diffraction blurs the image less
Its electrons have mass, so unlike photons they cannot be diffracted at all
Its electrons travel faster than light does, so the image forms more quickly
Its electrons have much longer wavelengths, so they spread out over the sample
questions.explanation: Electrons accelerated through thousands of volts have de Broglie wavelengths far smaller than visible light. A smaller λ/w ratio means less diffraction around fine structures, so smaller details can be resolved. Electrons do diffract, which is exactly why their wavelength matters.

questions.stem: Each photon in a beam of light has a wavelength of 500 nm. How much momentum does each photon carry? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
options: 0 kg m s⁻¹
4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹
3.3 × 10⁻⁴⁰ kg m s⁻¹
1.3 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Photons have no mass but do carry momentum: p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 500 × 10⁻⁹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹. 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the photon’s energy in joules, and multiplying h by λ gives 3.3 × 10⁻⁴⁰.

questions.stem: An electron and a photon have the same wavelength. Compared with the photon, the electron has:
options: less momentum, because it is slower
more momentum, because it has charge
the same momentum
more momentum, because it has mass
questions.explanation: For both light and matter, p = h/λ, so the same wavelength means the same momentum. The electron gets that momentum from its mass and speed, the photon from its energy, but the relationship with wavelength is identical.

questions.stem: Why does a sodium vapour lamp emit light only at certain wavelengths?
options: The sodium atoms inside it absorb every other wavelength of white light
The glass of the lamp filters out every wavelength except a few colours
Its electrons can have any energy, but they favour only a few of them
The electrons in its atoms can occupy only certain discrete energy levels
questions.explanation: Electrons in an atom can only have particular energies. When one drops from a higher level to a lower one, it emits a photon whose energy equals the difference, so only certain photon energies, and so certain wavelengths, appear. This is direct evidence of quantised energy levels.

questions.stem: White light passes through cool sodium vapour and is then spread into a spectrum. What does the spectrum show?
options: Dark lines at the same wavelengths as sodium’s emission lines
Bright lines at the same wavelengths as sodium’s emission lines
Dark lines at wavelengths different from its emission lines
A continuous spectrum of colours with no lines at all
questions.explanation: The atoms absorb only photons whose energy matches a gap between their energy levels, the same gaps that produce emission lines. Those wavelengths are removed from the white light, leaving dark absorption lines exactly where the bright emission lines would be.

questions.stem: An electron in an atom drops from an energy level of −1.5 eV to one of −3.4 eV. What is the energy of the photon emitted?
options: 1.9 eV
4.9 eV
3.4 eV
1.5 eV
questions.explanation: The photon carries the difference between the two levels: E = −1.5 − (−3.4) = 1.9 eV. Adding the magnitudes gives 4.9 eV, which mishandles the negative signs.

questions.stem: An electron moves between two energy levels in an atom that are 2.5 eV apart. What is the wavelength of the photon involved? Use h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: λ = hc/E = (4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/2.5 ≈ 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is green light. Using h in J s with an energy in eV gives 8.0 × 10⁻²⁶ m, and 6.0 × 10¹⁴ is the photon’s frequency in hertz, not a wavelength.

questions.stem: An atom has energy levels at −1.0 eV, −3.0 eV and −6.0 eV. Which photon energy could NOT be emitted as electrons fall between these levels?
options: 3.0 eV
5.0 eV
4.0 eV
2.0 eV
questions.explanation: The possible transitions are −1.0 to −3.0 (2.0 eV), −3.0 to −6.0 (3.0 eV) and −1.0 to −6.0 (5.0 eV). No pair of levels is 4.0 eV apart, so a 4.0 eV photon cannot be emitted.

questions.stem: Why was the idea of quantisation important to explaining the nature of atoms?
options: It explained why atoms emit and absorb only particular photon energies
It explained why atoms emit a continuous spread of every colour
It showed that electrons orbit at any radius with any energy
It showed that light travels only as a continuous electromagnetic wave
questions.explanation: If electrons in atoms could have any energy, atoms would emit continuous spectra. Line spectra showed that only certain energy differences occur, which quantised energy levels explain. Quantisation of light into photons, E = hf, was the same idea applied to light.

questions.stem: In a double slit experiment the light is so dim that only one photon passes through the apparatus at a time. What is seen on the detector after a very large number of photons have arrived?
options: An interference pattern built up from many individual dots
Two bright bands, one directly behind each of the two slits
No pattern at all, since a single photon cannot interfere
An even glow across the whole detector with no bands at all
questions.explanation: Each photon arrives at a single point, like a particle, but the points build up into bright and dark bands, like a wave. The interference pattern appears even though photons pass one at a time, which shows the wave behaviour belongs to each photon.

questions.stem: Electrons are sent one at a time towards a double slit. What do the results show about electrons?
options: They split in two, with half an electron passing through each of the slits
They arrive at single points like particles but build a wave interference pattern
They behave only as waves and spread evenly across the whole of the screen
They behave only as particles and form two bands directly behind the slits
questions.explanation: Each electron is detected at one point, a particle property, yet over time the arrivals form interference bands, a wave property. Like the single-photon experiment, this shows the dual nature of matter. Electrons are always detected whole, never as halves.
